title: The Voicemail
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Grief and communication with the dead
excerpt: The notification came in at 9:47 in the morning, on a Wednesday. Nueva mensaje de voz. Mamá. Her mother had died three years earlier. She had not appeared on Claudia's phone in three years. The message had a date. The date was yesterday.

chapters.title: A Missed Call
chapters.body:
The notification came in at 9:47 in the morning, on a Wednesday.

Claudia Restrepo was at her desk. She was, at the moment the notification came in, in the middle of a spreadsheet she had been working on since eight — a small quarterly reconciliation for the small architecture firm in Medellín where she had worked, for the last seven years, as the office manager and, more informally, as the person who kept the small ordinary chaos of a working design office from becoming disorderly. She was thirty-nine. She was, that Wednesday, thinking about lunch.

Her phone had, on the small desk beside her keyboard, buzzed once.

She had, without looking, reached for it.

She had unlocked it. She had, in the specific small habit of a woman who checked her phone perhaps ninety times a day, glanced at the small notification bar.

The notification had read: *Nueva mensaje de voz. Mamá.*

*New voice message. Mom.*

Claudia had, for a moment, not moved.

Her mother had died three years earlier. Her mother had died in November, of a small quick complication that had followed a small ordinary surgery, at the hospital in Medellín where she had been born and had lived and had, in the end, been treated. Her mother had, at the time of her death, been sixty-eight. Her mother had been, throughout Claudia's adult life, the person whose name had, more than any other, appeared on Claudia's phone.

She had not appeared, on Claudia's phone, in three years.

The small notification, on the small screen, had said: *Nueva mensaje de voz. Mamá.*

Claudia had, at the small desk in the small office, sat very still.

She had, at last, tapped on the notification.

The phone had opened the voicemail application. It had shown, at the top of the list, a new entry. The entry had had, in place of a caller identification, the specific small entry Claudia had, at some point in her life, saved for her mother — the small entry *Mamá* with a small green heart. It had had a small duration: *3:14.*

It had had a date.

The date had been *ayer* — yesterday. Tuesday. 4:22 in the afternoon.

Claudia had, at the small desk, looked at the date.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who did not entirely permit her mind to run ahead of her evidence, checked the date on her phone. The phone had confirmed: Wednesday, the current date, the current year. The message had been left, at the small time indicated, on the previous afternoon.

She had, in the specific small habit of the modern world, considered the possibility that this was some small system error. Voicemail systems sometimes, for reasons that were not always visible to their users, produced notifications for old messages. A three-year-old message might, in some obscure way, have been resurfaced. It might have been in the small database of the telephone company all this time, and might have been, in the previous afternoon, released to her account by some small glitch of software.

But the date had been *ayer.* Not November three years ago. Yesterday.

She had, on the small screen, tapped the small blue arrow to play the message.

She had held the phone to her ear.

The message had begun.

*Claudia,* her mother's voice had said. *Mija.*

Claudia had, at her desk, closed her eyes.

The voice had been, unmistakably, her mother's. It had been the specific small warm voice that had, throughout the whole of Claudia's life, been the voice that had, at every hour of every day, said her name in that specific way. She had, over three years, forgotten certain small features of the voice — the specific small pause her mother had put before certain words, the specific small chuckle that had accompanied certain other words — and the voice, on the small speaker at her ear, was reminding her of them all at once.

*Mija,* her mother had said. *Es tu madre.*

*It is your mother.*

*I am calling to say something small. It is not urgent. But it is not, either, unimportant. I would like you to listen to the whole message. Do not hang up in the middle. I will not, I promise, be long.*

Claudia had, at her desk, in the small quiet of the small office at nine forty-seven in the morning, listened.

*I am,* her mother had said, *in a small place that is difficult for me to describe. It is not, I do not think, exactly a place. It is, more precisely, a small time — a small stretch of time, before certain other things that I know are coming. I am, at this moment, alive. I do not know for how long. I do not know if I will speak to you again after this. I have been given the small opportunity to leave you this message. I have decided to use it.*

*I am not going to try to explain, mija, what has happened. I have not entirely understood it myself. I have understood only that this is, in some small careful way, my one chance to say the specific small things I have wanted, for some time, to say to you, and did not — during the last months of what you would call my life — quite manage.*

*The first small thing.*

*I would like you to know that I am not, in the small place I am in, unhappy. I have not been, in the years since I have been here, in any pain. I have not been in any small trouble. I have been, in the specific small careful way of a person in a small suspended time, at peace. You have, over the years since I have been gone, I know, been afraid for me — you have, in your specific small way of caring, been afraid that whatever came after was going to be difficult for me, or lonely, or frightening. It has not been. I do not know what it is. But it is not, in the small honest way of a woman who has spent the last several years in it, difficult.*

*I would like you to release, mija, whatever small worry you have been carrying about that.*

*The second small thing.*

*Your father.*

Claudia had, at her desk, made a small sound.

Her father had died when Claudia was seventeen. He had died, in the specific small terrible way of a man in his early forties, of a small quick heart attack in the small kitchen of the house Claudia had grown up in, on a Sunday morning in May. Her mother had, in the years that had followed, spoken about him rarely — in the specific small careful way of a woman who had loved a man and had lost him and had, for reasons of her own private grief, chosen to keep him quiet in her ordinary conversation.

*Your father,* her mother had said, *is here.*

*He was here when I arrived. He has been here, in the small time I have been in, with me. I want you to know this. I want you to know that whatever has happened, it has, at least, been the thing where I have him back. I have, in the last twenty-two years of what you would call my life, missed him more than I have ever told you. I have not been able to say this — I have not, throughout your childhood, been the sort of mother who could show you that kind of small private grief without frightening you. I have kept it. And now, in the small time I am in, I have him.*

*I would like you to know, mija, that whatever the small careful arrangement of this place is, it has, in the specific small way of a woman who has waited for a long time, been kind to me.*

*The third small thing.*

*I am not going to tell you when I will be gone from here. I do not know. I do not, in any specific way, know what will happen next. But I want you to know that if you do not hear from me again — if this is, as I suspect it may be, the only message I am ever going to be able to leave you — I have been, in the small time that I have had here, at peace. And I have, in the small time that I have had here, thought about you. I have thought about you every day. I have thought about you in the specific small way of a mother thinking about her daughter, which is a way of thinking that does not stop. It has not stopped for me here. It will not, so far as I can tell, stop.*

*I love you, mija.*

*I have always loved you.*

*I will, in whatever specific small way is available to me, go on loving you.*

*Do not, mija, live your life waiting for another message. I do not know that there will be one. Live your life. Marry, if you like. Do not, if you do not like. Have children, or do not. Do whatever it is you are going to do with the fifty or sixty years I hope you have left. Live them, mija.*

*I have loved you very much.*

*Goodbye, Claudia.*

*Goodbye.*

There had been, after the last *goodbye*, a small pause of perhaps five seconds. Then the small mechanical voice of the voicemail system had, in the small perfunctory way of that mechanical voice, said: *End of message. To repeat, press one. To delete —*

Claudia had, at her desk in the small quiet office at nine-fifty-two in the morning of a Wednesday, hung up the phone.

She had put the phone down on the desk.

She had, for a very long time, done nothing.

—

She had, at ten o'clock, gone to the small bathroom at the end of the corridor.

She had, in the small bathroom, washed her face at the sink. She had looked at herself, in the small mirror above the sink, for a moment. Her face, in the small mirror, had been the face of a woman who had, in the last ten minutes, received something she was going to have to think about for the rest of her life.

She had, at ten-oh-eight, come back to her desk.

She had picked up the phone.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman doing a small necessary check, opened the voicemail application again.

The message had, in the small list, been there. *Mamá. Ayer. 4:22 p.m. Duración: 3:14.*

The date had, on the second checking, remained: yesterday, Tuesday, at 4:22 in the afternoon.

She had tapped the small blue arrow again.

The message had played again.

It had been, on the second listening, the same message. The same voice. The same three small things. The same *goodbye.*

She had listened to it three more times over the course of the morning.

On the third listening she had, in the specific small careful way of a woman not permitting a small hope to seize her, noticed a small detail she had not, on the first listenings, been prepared to notice.

Her mother had said, at the beginning: *I am at this moment alive. I do not know for how long.*

Claudia had, sitting at her desk at eleven-fifteen on the Wednesday morning, understood what this meant.

She had understood that in the small time her mother was in — the small stretch of time, before whatever came next — her mother was, at the moment of leaving the message, not yet dead.

She had understood, with a specific small careful chill, that the small time her mother was in was, in some small way that was not visible from Claudia's ordinary Wednesday morning in Medellín, going to end. And that her mother — the small warm voice on the message, the specific small consciousness that was, at 4:22 on Tuesday afternoon, using her one chance to say what she had not said — was going to, at some future point, cease.

She had, in the specific small honest way of a woman considering this, understood that she had not, until this moment, believed her mother was continuing to exist anywhere.

She had understood, further, that she now had, in the specific small strange way of the last hour, evidence to the contrary.

She had understood, at last, that this evidence had come with an expiration.

Her mother was, at some point that Claudia could not identify, going to be gone in the small final way that Claudia had, for three years, believed her mother had been gone all along.

She was going to have to lose her mother a second time.

chapters.title: The Second Call
chapters.body:
She did not, at first, tell anyone.

She had considered, over the following days, telling her sister. Her sister Ana was two years older, lived in Bogotá with her husband and two small children, and had, throughout the last three years, been the one of the two sisters who had been in more regular contact with Claudia — the small weekly telephone call, the small biweekly video with the small nephews. Ana had, in the small careful way of an older sister, been Claudia's small ordinary support since their mother had died. Ana would, on being told about the message, believe her. Ana would want to hear it.

Claudia had, over those first days, thought about this carefully.

She had, in the end, decided not to.

She had decided not to because she had, in the small careful way of a woman who had received a small strange gift, understood that the message was, in some small specific way she could not entirely articulate, hers. Her mother had left it to her. Her mother had not left one to Ana. The voicemail application had, in the last three days, produced no notification for Ana. If it had, Ana would have called Claudia by now. Ana had not.

She had, on the fourth day, come to a small careful understanding of this fact.

She had understood that her mother had, in the small careful way of a woman using her one chance, chosen. She had chosen Claudia. She had not, so far as Claudia could tell, chosen Ana. This was not, Claudia thought as she considered it, a matter of preference — Claudia did not think her mother had loved her more, or Ana less. It was a matter of the specific small strange arrangement of the moment. Her mother had had one call. She had made it to one number. She had picked one daughter.

Claudia had, on the fourth day, understood that she was the one who had been picked.

She had also understood, on the fourth day, that this made her responsible for what to do with the picking.

She had considered, over the following week, what she could do. She had considered telling Ana anyway, in the specific small careful way of a sister who wanted to share what she had received. She had considered playing the recording to Ana over the phone, so that Ana could hear their mother's voice at least once more, three years after.

She had, however, understood over those days a small other thing.

She had understood that if she played the message for Ana, Ana would want the message. Ana would want to keep it. Ana would ask, in the small specific way of a bereaved sister, whether the message was going to be preserved, whether Claudia was going to send her a copy, whether they could, together, hold onto it.

And Claudia had, in the small honest way of a woman who had listened to the message twenty times over the last four days, understood that she did not want to keep a copy. She did not want to preserve it. She did not, in the small careful way of a woman who had received a specific small warning at the end of the message — *live your life, do not wait for another* — want the message to become the specific small object around which the rest of her life arranged itself.

She had understood, on the seventh day, that her mother had, in leaving the message, been asking her to *listen* to it, not to *keep* it.

She had, on the eighth day, listened to the message once more.

She had, at the end of that listening, deleted it.

She had done it in the specific small careful way of a woman doing something she had thought about for a long time. She had opened the voicemail application. She had held down the entry. She had, at the prompt asking whether she was sure, said yes. She had, at the second prompt confirming permanent deletion, said yes.

The message had, on the small screen, disappeared.

She had, that evening, sat on the small balcony of her small apartment in Poblado and had watched the small yellow lights come on in the small buildings on the small hill opposite. She had, for a long moment, been afraid that she had done a specific small terrible thing.

She had, at last, understood that she had done what her mother had asked.

—

She had, in the following weeks, tried to live her life.

She had gone to work. She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had not been able to marry, had a small pleasant date with a small pleasant man from a small pleasant application. She had, on a Saturday, gone with Ana and the small nephews to the small park in Envigado where they had, throughout their childhood, gone with their mother. She had, at the small park, watched her small nephews play, and had thought about her mother in the specific small careful way of a daughter who had received a small careful goodbye.

She had, at the small park, understood that her mother would have wanted this. She had, at the small park, been at peace.

She had gone home. She had, that evening, cooked herself a small dinner. She had, at ten, gone to bed.

She had, at eleven-thirteen, been woken by her phone.

The phone had, on the small bedside table, buzzed once.

She had reached for it in the dark.

The notification had read: *Nueva mensaje de voz. Mamá.*

—

She had sat up in the small dark of her bedroom.

She had, for a long moment, held the phone.

She had, at last, opened the voicemail application. The new entry was at the top of the list. Duration: 47 seconds. Date: today, at 11:11 in the evening.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman whose hands were shaking slightly, tapped the small blue arrow.

The message had begun.

*Mija.*

Her mother's voice. Slightly quieter than the first message. Slightly slower.

*I am — I am not sure how much time I have. I am, at this moment, in the small time still. But I am — I am aware, in some way I did not expect, that this is not going to last very much longer. I do not know how I know. But I know.*

*I have found that I am able, in the small careful way you have understood, to leave you a second message.*

*I do not know why I am able. I had thought that the first was the only one. But I am here. And so I am going to say what I have.*

*Mija, I need to ask you something.*

There had been, at that point in the message, a small pause. Perhaps three seconds.

*I need to ask you not to try to contact me.*

Claudia had, in the small dark of her bedroom, held the phone very still.

*I do not,* her mother had said, *know what you have been doing since you received the first message. I do not know if you have — if you have been trying to reach me. If you have been visiting my grave. If you have been going to any specific small place where you thought you might, in some way, get closer. I do not know. But I am asking you now to stop, if you have been doing any of these things.*

*I am asking because I have understood, in the small time since I left you the first message, that the small connection between us is — is fragile. I do not know how to describe this. I have understood that I am, in the small time I am in, at a specific small distance from you. And that if I try to close the distance — or if you try to close it — the small time I am in becomes shorter. Every attempt to reach across the distance costs me time.*

*The first message cost me a great deal of time.*

*I have understood, in the last several days, that I had — I had not known, when I left the first message, how much it would cost. If I had known, I do not know if I would have left it. I have thought about this. I have decided that I would have. I have decided that the first message was worth the cost.*

*The second message — this one — is costing me the rest, mija.*

*I am leaving it because I need you to know. I need you to not — not do anything that would call me back. I need you to live the life I asked you to live in the first message. I need you to let me — let me go the rest of the way.*

*I do not, mija, want you to feel guilty. I do not know what you have been doing since the first message. It may be that you have done nothing. It may be that the small connection has been closing on its own, without any small action from you. I do not know. I only know that I am, at this moment, almost gone, and that I do not have — I do not have another message in me. I would like this one to be the last.*

*I love you, mija. I have loved you very much. I have loved you always. I —*

There had been, at that word, a small silence.

The small silence had lasted, so far as Claudia could tell in the specific small dark of the bedroom, for perhaps ten seconds.

Then the mechanical voice had said: *End of message.*

—

Claudia had, in the small dark of her bedroom, sat with the phone in her lap for a very long time.

She had, at last, understood something.

She had understood that her mother — the small warm consciousness that had, on the previous Tuesday, been in some small suspended time and had used her one chance to leave a small careful message — had not, in the small time since, been at rest. She had, at some point in the last week, become aware that a further message was possible. She had tried. She had, in the trying, used up the small last of the small time she had had.

Claudia had not, in the small careful way she had lived over the past week, done anything to try to contact her mother. She had not visited her mother's grave. She had not gone to any small place. She had, on the whole, tried to do what her mother had asked in the first message — to live her life. She had thought about her mother, of course. She had thought about her mother, in the specific small warm way of a daughter who had received a small careful goodbye, every day.

She had understood, sitting in the small dark of her bedroom at eleven-thirty on a Sunday evening, that even the small warm thinking had, in the small careful arrangement of the connection, been costing her mother something. Not much. Not, perhaps, very much. But something. Every specific small thought of her mother, over the past week, had been a small careful drawing on the small remaining time her mother had had. Every listening to the first message. Every small warm moment at the small park in Envigado.

And her mother, in the small careful way of a mother, had permitted it. Had understood it as the specific small ordinary cost of a daughter's love, and had not, until she had almost run out, said anything.

She had said it now.

She had said it because she had understood that if she did not say it, Claudia would go on with her small warm thinking, and her mother would go on paying the small careful cost, and at some point the cost would exceed what her mother had, and her mother would, in some specific small way Claudia could not imagine, be — she used the word she had used — *gone.*

Claudia had understood, sitting in the small dark of her bedroom, that her mother had, in this second message, been asking her to *stop.*

Not to stop loving. Not to stop remembering. Not to stop any small ordinary work of a daughter's grief.

Only to stop the small specific attention that was, in some way she did not entirely understand, reaching across the small distance.

Claudia had understood that this was, in the specific small careful way of a mother's love, the last favor her mother was going to ask her.

She had understood that she was going to do it.

chapters.title: The Distance
chapters.body:
She had, over the following weeks, tried to learn how to stop.

She had discovered, in the specific small careful way of a woman learning a small strange discipline, that it was harder than she had thought.

The small warm thinking was not, she had understood over those weeks, a thing one did deliberately. It was, more precisely, a thing one *was*. The specific small attention she had — that any daughter had — for a dead mother was not an activity that could, by any small careful decision, be switched off. It was the specific small ongoing presence of the mother in the daughter's ordinary awareness — in the specific small moments of the daughter's day, in the specific small habits the daughter had inherited from the mother, in the specific small feelings the daughter had that came, in some small quiet way, from the mother's specific small teaching.

Claudia had, on the third day after the second message, understood that she could not, in any specific way, stop.

She had understood, further, that if she could not stop, her mother was going to continue to pay the small careful cost. That whatever remaining time her mother had, in the small suspended place with her father, was being drawn on by Claudia's ongoing existence as a woman who had loved her mother.

Claudia had, on the third day, wept.

She had wept in the small quiet of her small apartment at eleven at night. She had wept because she had understood that the specific small arrangement she was in was one that could not be resolved by any small careful action. She could not, by any specific small decision, keep her mother in the small suspended time. Her mother had already made the decision. Her mother was, at whatever small remaining rate the small connection permitted, being drawn on. And Claudia's specific small warm ordinary love was, in some small careful way, the specific thing doing the drawing.

She had, on the fourth day, considered whether she should ask her mother to stop leaving messages.

She had understood, in the small careful way she had come to consider these things, that this was not the specific small problem. Her mother had said, in the second message, that she was not going to leave another. Her mother had not been asking Claudia to prevent further messages. Her mother had been asking Claudia to prevent something else. To prevent the specific small ongoing pulling across the distance that Claudia had, in the ordinary work of her ordinary love, been doing.

Claudia had, on the fifth day, tried a specific small thing.

She had, at three in the afternoon on a Wednesday, sat down at the small round table in her small kitchen. She had put a small notebook in front of her. She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman doing a small difficult thing, written on the top of a fresh page:

*Mamá,*

*I do not know if you can hear this. I do not know if writing it costs you anything. If it does, I am sorry. I will not write again after this.*

*I have understood what you asked me to do. I do not know if I can do it in the way you asked. I do not know if the specific small attention I have for you is a thing that can be — that can be stopped. I have tried, in the last week, and I have not been able to. I have understood, in trying, that the specific small attention I have for you is, in the specific small way of a daughter, the small permanent shape of who I am.*

*I would like to ask you something.*

*I would like to ask you to please, if it is possible, go the rest of the way now. Do not wait for me to stop the small attention. I cannot stop it. I have tried. If I cannot stop it, and it is costing you time, please — please use whatever remaining time you have to go, rather than to wait. I do not want you to spend your last remaining time in the small suspended place trying to accommodate me. I want you to go and be with father. I want you to have whatever comes after. I do not want you to be trapped in the small suspended place because your daughter cannot stop thinking about you.*

*I love you, mama. I will always love you. But I am asking you to please go.*

*Your Claudia.*

She had, at the small round table, closed the notebook.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman doing a small ritual, taken the notebook to the small balcony of the apartment, and had, in the specific small careful way, torn out the page. She had, using the small book of matches she kept in a drawer for the small candles she sometimes lit, set fire to the page over the small ceramic bowl she kept on the balcony for occasional small purposes.

She had watched the page burn.

She had watched it burn until it had been only small grey ash in the small ceramic bowl.

She had, that evening, made herself a small dinner. She had eaten it. She had gone to bed at eleven. She had, at eleven-thirteen — the specific time of the second message — held her breath.

The phone had not, at eleven-thirteen, buzzed.

The phone had not, at any point during the night, buzzed.

She had, at some point around one in the morning, slept.

—

She had, over the following weeks, not received another message.

She had, in the small careful way of a woman living her life, gone about her ordinary business. She had worked. She had, on a Saturday, gone again with Ana to the park in Envigado. She had, in the specific small careful way she had learned, thought about her mother, and had not tried to stop thinking about her, and had — in the specific small honest way she had come, over those weeks, to understand — stopped worrying about whether the specific small thinking was costing her mother anything.

She had understood that the specific small letter she had burned on the balcony had been received.

She had understood that her mother had, in the small careful way of a woman doing what her daughter had, at last, asked her to do, gone.

She had understood, in the specific small careful way of a woman not permitting herself a certainty she could not have, that this was probably right.

—

She had, at some point in the following autumn, told Ana about the messages.

She had done this in the specific small careful way she had thought about doing it, over the small months since she had received them. She had told Ana, over a small dinner in Ana's small kitchen in Bogotá, on a small evening when the small nephews had been asleep and the small husband had been out. She had told Ana simply. She had told Ana what the messages had said. She had told Ana that she had, in the end, deleted them.

Ana had, for a long moment, looked at her.

Ana had said, at last: *why did you not tell me.*

Claudia had said: *because I was — I did not know what I had. I did not know if it was real. And by the time I had understood, I had also understood that mother had — that mother had spent her small remaining time on the messages, and that if I told you, you would want more, and I could not give you more.*

Ana had said, quietly: *I would not have asked for more.*

Claudia had said: *you would have. I would have. Anyone would have.*

Ana had, at this, been quiet.

Ana had said, at last: *did she say anything about me.*

Claudia had, at the small kitchen table, understood that this was the small question Ana had been carrying since Claudia had begun to speak.

She had said, quietly: *she said — she said she thought about all of us. Every day. In the specific small way of a mother thinking about her daughters. I do not remember, mija — I do not remember whether she said your name. But she — I would say — she said everything, in the small careful way of a mother saying everything to whoever happens to be in the room. It was for both of us.*

Ana had, for a moment, been quiet.

Ana had said, at last: *thank you.*

Ana had said: *thank you for telling me. Even now. Even after.*

Claudia had said: *I should have told you sooner.*

Ana had said: *maybe. But — but you did what she asked. You did the small strange thing. You let her go. I do not — I do not think, in your position, I would have been able to. I think I would have kept her.*

Claudia had said, quietly: *she was mother.*

Ana had said: *yes.*

They had, at the small kitchen table, sat together for a very long time.

—

Claudia had, over the following decades, lived her life.

She had not, at any point in those decades, received another message from her mother. She had not received one from her father. She had not received any other small strange communication from any dead person she had ever known.

She had lived, in the specific small careful way her mother had asked her to live, an ordinary life. She had not, in the end, married. She had, at forty-three, adopted a small girl from a small orphanage in Cali, and had raised her, and had, in the small careful way of a mother, done for the small girl what her own mother had done for her.

She had, in her small careful old age, told her small adopted daughter about the messages once.

She had told her daughter this on the small anniversary of her mother's death, in the specific small quiet way of an old woman telling a small important story to a small careful younger woman who was, by then, an adult with a small family of her own.

Her daughter had listened.

Her daughter had, at the end, said: *did you ever wish you had kept the recordings.*

Claudia had said: *every day.*

Her daughter had said: *and did you ever regret deleting them.*

Claudia had said: *no.*

Her daughter had said: *how can both of those be true.*

Claudia had said: *because they are two different things, mija. One is a small wish. The other is a small decision. The wish is the small ordinary wish of a woman who loved her mother. The decision was the small honest decision of a woman who had understood what her mother wanted. Both can be true at the same time. Most of the important things in a life are like that.*

Her daughter had, at that, been quiet for a while.

Her daughter had said, at last: *and if it happens to me.*

Claudia had said: *what.*

Her daughter had said: *if I — if, when you are gone, I receive a message from you. What do you want me to do.*

Claudia had, at the small kitchen table, understood the small careful question her daughter had been carrying since Claudia had begun the story.

She had said, quietly: *listen to it once, mija. Then delete it. Do not, if you can help it, think too hard about it after. Let me — let me go the rest of the way.*

Her daughter had, at this, quietly wept.

Her daughter had said: *I do not know if I will be able to.*

Claudia had said: *I know. I did not know either. But you do it anyway, mija. You do it because it is what I am asking. You do it because — because it is, in the specific small careful way of a mother's last request, the last kindness I will ever ask of you. You do it, and then you go on with your life, and you do not, in the small strange way of a daughter who has received a small strange message, wait for another. You live. You raise your children. You grow old.*

*And you do not, mija, wait for me.*

Her daughter had, at the small kitchen table, held her mother's hand.

They had sat together.

—

Claudia had died, at seventy-eight, of a small quiet stroke, in the small quiet way of a woman who had lived a small careful life. She had died in her small apartment in Poblado, where she had lived for the whole of her adult life, on a small clear morning in September.

Her daughter had, three days later, received a small notification on her small phone.

The notification had read: *Nueva mensaje de voz. Mamá.*

Her daughter had, at the small kitchen table of her small apartment in Bogotá, held the phone.

She had, for a very long time, considered.

She had, at last, tapped on the notification. She had opened the voicemail. She had listened to the message. She had heard, in her mother's specific small warm voice, the small careful things her mother had, at some small suspended time in some small suspended place, taken her one chance to say.

She had, at the end of the message, sat with it for a long moment.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman doing what her mother had asked, deleted it.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had, at last, understood what her mother had meant by the whole strange story, wept.

She had gone on with her life.

She had lived, in the small careful way her mother had asked her to live, an ordinary life.

Her mother had, so far as she knows, gone the rest of the way.
